passage: Sit, Chinmay. You said yesterday that you go to your father's flat and come home angry, so Thomas uncle will tell you what he did. Not a lecture. When I was twenty-five my father fell and needed help every morning. This was the man who never once came to my school and called me lazy at every dinner. I went daily and did the work, and under my skin I was furious. What I learned was that I could bring his food and still say, "I will not sit through the insults." The first time I said it, he went quiet, and after some weeks he stopped. I also spoke to a counsellor, which took me a year to admit I needed. I never forgave him in one clean moment. But I could look after him without pretending the old days had not happened.

qa.q: How old was Thomas when his father fell?
qa.a: Thomas was twenty-five when his father fell.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling while he did his father's daily care, and how do you know?
qa.a: He was furious underneath, as he says himself, because of the old hurt of being called lazy and never being visited at school.

qa.q: What two things let Thomas keep caring for his father without swallowing the hurt?
qa.a: He set a limit, saying he would not sit through the insults, and he talked to a counsellor about the past.

qa.q: How might Chinmay feel hearing this after what Chinmay said about visiting the father's flat?
qa.a: Chinmay may feel relieved and less alone, hearing that caring for a parent and staying angry about the past can exist together.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how he cared for a hurtful parent while holding a boundary and seeking support for old childhood hurt.

The monsoon had turned the hospital road into a river, and the clinic token queue was already forty long when Nazia got her mother Damini there, both soaked to the knees.

"You never could plan anything," Damini said.

Nazia felt the old heat rise. She had heard some version of that sentence her whole childhood: about her grades, her friends, her cooking. She still took her mother to every appointment, still sorted her tablets each Sunday.

Now she took a breath. "Ammi, I'll wait here with you as long as it takes. But if you keep saying things like that, I'll wait outside."

Damini pressed her lips together. They sat in silence for an hour.

That evening Nazia wrote in the notebook her counsellor had suggested: "I can care for her and still protect myself. I don't have to forgive everything today."

Then she set the alarm for Thursday's blood test.

qa.q: How long was the clinic token queue when they arrived?
qa.a: The queue was already forty long.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Damini said she could never plan anything?
qa.a: Nazia felt the old hurt and anger rise, since she had heard that kind of criticism throughout her childhood.

qa.q: How did Nazia hold a boundary while still caring for Damini?
qa.a: She calmly said she would stay but would wait outside if the insults continued, and she kept processing the past with her counsellor.

qa.q: How might Damini see the boundary Nazia set?
qa.a: Damini may feel stung or surprised, pressing her lips together, but she chose silence over more criticism.

grounding: Shows a young woman caring for a parent while carrying childhood hurt, holding boundaries and processing the past with support.

passage:
After Vishal Deshmukh broke his hip, his daughter Nandini moved back into her old room in the Thane flat for six weeks.

It was strange to cook his upma in the kitchen where he used to shout at her for spilling milk. He had missed every school play, every prize day. Now he called her twenty times a day.

She did the care well: medicines at eight, physiotherapy at eleven, fresh sheets on Sundays. But when he started criticising her husband's job, she put down the tray. "Papa, I'm here to help you. I'm not going to listen to that." She walked out, came back ten minutes later with his tea, and changed the subject.

At night she called a helpline for carers once, just to say out loud that she was tired and angry and also loved him. The volunteer said all three could be true.

On the last day, Vishal said, "You're good at this." Nandini didn't know what to feel.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when Vishal said, "You're good at this"?
qa.a: Nandini felt confused and mixed, with old hurt from childhood alongside a small warmth at the praise.

qa.q: What did Nandini do to hold a boundary while still caring for her father?
qa.a: She calmly refused to listen to criticism of her husband, left briefly, returned with tea, and sought support from a carers' helpline.

qa.q: How might Vishal experience Nandini's care during those six weeks?
qa.a: Vishal seems dependent and perhaps grateful, calling often and finally praising her, though he may not realise the old hurt she carries.

grounding: Shows a young woman caring for a father who hurt her in childhood, holding boundaries and processing the past with support.
